# Feature engineering {#sec-features} ## The as-of rule A feature for a game may only use games **played before it**. Using the game's own result, or anything later, is *leakage*: the backtest looks great and the model fails in real life. In practice, features are computed per **slate** (season, season type, week) from earlier slates only. A Saturday game never sees Thursday's result from the same week, which also matches what's known when lines are bet midweek. The rule is enforced by a test (`tests/test_features.py`): building the features with every future result **hidden** must produce exactly the same values as building them with full data. Both the score-based and the CFBD-based features pass it. Only FBS-vs-FBS games feed ratings and form; FCS blowouts would distort them. ## Opponent-adjusted ratings Scoring 40 against a bad defense isn't the same as scoring 40 against a good one. The core feature, following @cfbd_ridge, solves for every offense and defense at once. Before each slate $s$, fit on prior team-games $i$: $$ \text{points}_i \;=\; \mu \;+\; o_{\text{team}(i)} \;-\; d_{\text{opp}(i)} \;+\; h \cdot \text{hfa}_i \;+\; \varepsilon_i, \qquad \text{hfa}_i \in \{+1, 0, -1\}, $$ where $o$ is offensive strength, $d$ defensive strength (higher is better), and $h$ the home edge. Coefficients are estimated with **ridge regression** and **recency weights**: $$ \min_{\mu, o, d, h} \; \sum_i w_i \big(\text{points}_i - \hat{\text{points}}_i\big)^2 \;+\; \alpha \big(\lVert o \rVert^2 + \lVert d \rVert^2 + h^2\big), \qquad w_i = 2^{-\text{age}_i / \tau}, $$ with $\text{age}_i$ in days and half-life $\tau$. The training window is 600 days, so in September last season acts as the prior, and current form takes over as games accumulate. Ridge shrinks teams with little data toward average. The model's own prediction for a matchup is $$ \text{exp\_points} = \mu + o_{\text{team}} - d_{\text{opp}} + h \cdot \text{hfa}. $$ ### Tuning α and τ ::: {#tbl-ridge-grid .cell tbl-cap='MAE of exp_points alone (team points, 2017–2023) for each shrinkage α and recency half-life τ (days).' execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
half-life 60 120 240
alpha
0.3 9.96 9.59 9.61
1.0 9.84 9.55 9.56
3.0 9.94 9.69 9.61
8.0 10.27 10.04 9.87
``` ::: ::: $\alpha = 1$, $\tau = 120$ days wins. Heavy shrinkage ($\alpha = 8$) squeezes every team toward average; a short memory ($\tau = 60$) forgets last season too fast for September. An early version used $\alpha = 25$ and compressed every rating to about ±1 point; that bug and its fix are in @sec-decisions. The same machinery is reused for **any per-game offensive stat** (plays, EPA per play, success rate, explosiveness, pass and rush EPA). The target is standardized before fitting, so $\alpha$ means the same shrinkage for every stat; coefficients are returned in the stat's own units. ## Elo with a nonlinear margin of victory A second rating, FiveThirtyEight-style [@fte_elo]. After each game, $$ R' = R + K \cdot M \cdot (S - E), \qquad E = \frac{1}{1 + 10^{-\Delta/400}}, \qquad M = \ln(|\text{MOV}| + 1) \cdot \frac{2.2}{0.001\,\Delta_w + 2.2}, $$ with $K = 25$, home edge 55 Elo points, and one-third regression to 1500 each offseason. The logarithm gives diminishing credit for blowouts (a 40-point win is worth little more than a 30-point win). The second factor corrects autocorrelation: favorites win by more, which would otherwise inflate their rating [@morse_elo]. ## Feature families ::: {#tbl-families .cell tbl-cap='Feature families and their sizes.' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
features what
raw_form 11 points for/against, season-to-date and last 3,...
ratings 7 ridge offense/defense for team and opponent, e...
elo 3 Elo, opponent Elo, difference
matchup 9 explicit interactions: off × opp_def, expected...
context 9 neutral site, conference game, rest days and d...
efficiency 30 ridge-adjusted tempo, EPA/play, success rate, ...
pace_x_efficiency 3 expected plays × expected EPA/play, game pace,...
priors 8 talent composite and returning production, tea...
preseason 13 transfer portal, recruiting classes, new head ...
``` ::: ::: ## Which families earn their place? Walk-forward cross-validation (train on every season before, validate on each of 2019–2023; @sec-modeling). Families are added one at a time. Ridge is linear; "LightGBM on residual" learns `points − exp_points`, so the ratings carry the signal and the trees correct what they miss. ::: {#tbl-ablation .cell tbl-cap='Cross-validated MAE (points per team, 2019–2023) as feature families are added.' execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
Ridge LightGBM on residual
baseline: league average 11.09 —
ratings formula alone 9.44 —
market: closing line 8.91 —
raw_form 10.02 9.44
+ratings 9.44 9.45
+elo 9.44 9.44
+matchup 9.44 9.44
+context 9.44 9.43
+efficiency 9.41 9.38
+pace_x_efficiency 9.41 9.38
+priors 9.33 9.31
+preseason 9.30 9.28
``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Error as families are added (LightGBM on residual), against the league-average baseline and the closing line.](features_files/figure-pdf/fig-ablation-output-1.pdf){#fig-ablation} ::: ::: Note: the "LightGBM on residual" column always starts from the ratings' prediction (it learns `points − exp_points`), so even its `raw_form` row already contains the ratings. That's why it starts near 9.44, not near 10. The reading: - **Opponent adjustment is the big win.** The league average misses by ~11.1; the ratings alone by ~9.44. Raw form (unadjusted points) only reaches ~10.0. - Elo, explicit matchup terms and context add almost nothing on top of the ratings. - **CFBD efficiency** helps a bit (~9.38), and **talent and returning production** help most among the new families (~9.30), mainly by fixing early weeks. - The explicit pace × efficiency product adds nothing: trees already combine plays and efficiency on their own. - The **closing line** is still better (~8.91). The gap is information, not model complexity, which is what @sec-nonlinearity investigates.
